Atlantic herring Clupea harengus embryos undergo development within a delicate, transparent chorion until eclosion occurs. Laboratory studies conducted at a controlled temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C] have documented that hatching takes place after approximately 27 days [ab = approximately 27 days], a period that reflects the relatively slow metabolic rates characteristic of cool-water clupeids. Upon emergence, the prolarva measures just 1.1 cm [Lb = 1.1 cm] in total length, representing the yolk-sac larval stage when the individual remains entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves. This stage is critical as it bridges the transition from embryonic nutrition to the onset of exogenous feeding. At this diminutive size, the newly hatched larva is poorly developed, lacking a functional mouth and relying on its yolk supply for energy. The duration of this lecithotrophic phase is tightly linked to temperature; at the experimental incubation temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C] recorded in the same laboratory measurements, the yolk is absorbed slowly, prolonging the period before the larva must successfully capture its first planktonic prey.

Following yolk-sac resorption, the exotrophic larva embarks on a pelagic phase characterized by rapid growth and morphological differentiation. The larval metamorphosis, a dramatic transformation involving fin ray ossification, scale formation, and the transition from a planktonic to a more juvenile body plan, occurs at an age of approximately 177 days  under a thermal regime of 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This temperature, typical of North Sea nursery grounds during the summer months, accelerates developmental rates compared to cooler environments. During the pre-metamorphic period, the larva remains a transparent, free-swimming member of the ichthyoplankton community, feeding on copepods and other small zooplankton. The timing of metamorphosis is not fixed but varies with local conditions; however, the value of 177 days  provides a robust estimate for populations inhabiting temperate waters at 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. The completion of metamorphosis marks the recruitment of the individual into the juvenile stage, at which point it begins to assume the more streamlined, silvery appearance characteristic of adult Atlantic herring.

Attainment of puberty in Atlantic herring is a gradual process influenced by both size and environmental conditions. Field surveys and otolith-based studies indicate that the mean total length at which 50% of individuals become sexually mature is 29 cm [Lp = 29 cm]. This length is reached at an age of approximately 4 years after hatching [tR = approximately 4 years after hatching] when measured under the prevailing thermal conditions of the North Sea at 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. The interpretation of this age as the onset of first reproduction rather than merely the onset of gonadal recrudescence is supported by histological evidence of active spawning in individuals of this size class. It is worth noting that some herring biologists consider this estimate to be on the later side, as anecdotal reports from commercial catches sometimes indicate first-time spawners as young as 2 years. Nevertheless, the value of 4 years [tR = 4 years] after hatching remains the most robustly documented benchmark from long-term survey data, and it aligns with the species' iteroparous, batch-spawning life history.

Estimated from fecundity studies on gravid females, the highest recorded fecundity reaches approximately 55 eggs per day, which corresponds to approximately 20,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 20,000 eggs per year] when sustained over the course of a protracted spawning season at an average water temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This rate underscores the high reproductive potential of this species, and it is derived from a combination of batch fecundity counts and spawning frequency data, though the temperature value of 11 °C [T = 11 °C] remains tentative given the variability in thermal regimes across the species' range. The ultimate body size that a herring can achieve is a related metric; the maximum recorded adult body mass in the IMARES database is 1050 grams [Wwi = 1050 grams], though such large individuals are rare and are typically found in market samples rather than in routine survey catches.

Longevity in Atlantic herring is constrained by both natural mortality and fishing pressure, but maximum lifespan estimates provide insight into the species' intrinsic physiological limits. The oldest individual documented in the IMARES database reached an age of 22 years [am = 22 years], a value that was obtained from otolith readings of a market sample collected from the North Sea at a long-term average temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This figure is notably higher than the 13 to 20 years more commonly observed in survey data and reflects the potential for exceptional longevity under favorable conditions. In terms of terminal size, the ultimate total length reported for the species is 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], a length attained by only the oldest and largest individuals in the population. These metrics of lifespan and maximum length together define the upper bounds of the herring's life history, against which the earlier life stages—from the 1.1 cm [Lb = 1.1 cm] neonate to the 29 cm [Lp = 29 cm] maturing adult—can be placed in context. The species thus exhibits a classic k-selected strategy, with slow maturation, high fecundity, and the capacity for considerable longevity.
